questions.q: What does at-least-once delivery guarantee?
options: Every message is delivered exactly one time to exactly one consumer
Every message is eventually delivered, though consumers may see duplicates
Messages may be dropped, but any delivered message arrives only once
Messages arrive in the exact order producers originally sent them

questions.q: In pub/sub, what happens when a message is published to a topic?
options: It goes to a single subscriber selected round-robin for fairness
It is stored until one subscriber explicitly requests and removes it
It is routed only to the subscriber that has been idle the longest
Every subscription attached to the topic receives its own copy

questions.q: What is the purpose of a consumer group (as in Kafka)?
options: To share a topic's partitions among members so each message is handled once per group
To duplicate every message to every member so the group tolerates individual crashes
To batch acknowledgements from many consumers into one network round trip
To encrypt traffic between the broker and a trusted set of consumers

questions.q: What is a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for?
options: Holding messages whose TTL expired before any consumer came online
Archiving every successfully processed message for compliance audits
Parking messages that repeatedly failed processing for later inspection
Buffering messages during broker restarts so none are dropped

questions.q: What is the core difference between a queue and a pub/sub topic?
options: Queues always preserve strict global ordering while topics deliver messages in arbitrary order
A queue delivers each message to one consumer; a topic fans out to many subscribers
Topics persist messages to disk while queues are strictly memory-only
Queues scale horizontally while topics are limited to a single broker

questions.q: Why do brokers require consumer acknowledgements?
options: So a message can be redelivered if the consumer dies before finishing it
So the broker can bill producers accurately for each delivered message
So consumers can veto messages they consider malformed or hostile
So the broker knows when to compress older segments of the log

questions.q: What does backpressure mean in a messaging pipeline?
options: Consumers replay old messages backward to rebuild corrupted state
The broker transparently compresses queued messages whenever its memory begins running low
Producers retry failed sends with exponentially growing delays
Downstream slowness propagates upstream, forcing producers to slow or buffer

questions.q: Where is ordering typically guaranteed in Kafka-style logs?
options: Across the whole topic regardless of how many partitions it has
Across all topics owned by the same producer application
Within a single partition, for messages sharing that partition
Nowhere; consumers must reorder using timestamps in each message

questions.q: A consumer crashes after processing but before acking. With at-least-once delivery, what happens?
options: The message is redelivered and gets processed a second time
The broker detects completion via a heartbeat and drops the message
The message routes straight to the DLQ as a poisoned message
The whole partition pauses until the crashed consumer rejoins

questions.q: Orders for each customer must be processed in sequence, with high throughput overall. Best approach?
options: Use a single partition for the entire topic to enforce global order
Attach sequence numbers and have every consumer buffer and reorder events indefinitely
Partition by customer ID so each customer's events stay in one ordered stream
Timestamp each event and rely on the broker to sort before delivery

questions.q: One member of a Kafka consumer group is much slower than the rest. What is the effect?
options: The broker shrinks its partition count until the slow member recovers
Other members steal individual messages from the slow member's partitions
The group coordinator throttles fast members so all progress evenly
Lag builds on its partitions while other members' partitions stay current

questions.q: A message keeps failing and being redelivered forever (a poison pill). What is the standard remedy?
options: Lower the broker's replication factor so the message expires faster
Cap retry attempts, then route the message to a dead-letter queue
Skip acknowledgements entirely so the broker stops redelivering it
Restart the consumer group so offsets reset past the bad message

questions.q: Why can an exactly-once delivery claim be misleading?
options: Brokers cannot deduplicate anything because unique message identifiers get stripped during transit
It requires perfectly synchronized clocks, which no realistic distributed system can provide
It typically means effectively-once via dedup or transactions, not zero duplicates on the wire
It only works when there is exactly one producer and one consumer

questions.q: Producers outpace consumers for hours and queue depth keeps growing. Which mitigation attacks the root cause?
options: Raise the broker's disk quota so the backlog can grow for longer
Shorten message TTLs so old work silently expires from the queue
Enable gzip compression so the backlog fits in less memory
Scale out consumers or shed load at the producer side

questions.q: Why prefer log-based brokers (Kafka) over classic queues for event sourcing and replay?
options: Consumers keep offsets into a retained log, so history can be re-read at will
Log brokers push messages faster because they skip consumer acknowledgements
Classic queues cannot fan a message out to more than one consumer
Log brokers guarantee global ordering across every partition and topic

questions.q: Twelve services need the same order events. Why publish once to a topic rather than send twelve queue messages?
options: Queues would reorder the events differently for every downstream team
Producers stay decoupled from the subscriber list, which can change freely
Topic delivery is guaranteed exactly-once while queue delivery is not
A topic lets subscribers share one consumer offset, halving broker storage

questions.q: Frequent consumer restarts cause repeated Kafka rebalances. What is the impact and mitigation?
options: Every in-flight message is permanently lost during each rebalance; enabling producer idempotence recovers them
Offsets reset to zero each time; shrink retention so replay stays cheap
The broker leader flaps; move the cluster to a single beefier broker
Processing pauses during reassignment; use cooperative rebalancing and static membership

questions.q: You need strict ordering AND horizontal scale for a payments stream. What is the realistic design?
options: Global FIFO across the entire topic, achieved by routing all traffic through a single partition and consumer
Per-key ordering: partition by account so each account is sequential while accounts run in parallel
Broker-side reordering driven by synchronized timestamps across all producers
Consumer-side sorting with a five-minute buffering window before applying events

questions.q: An at-least-once consumer writes to a non-idempotent downstream API. What is the safest pattern?
options: Deduplicate with a persisted processed-ID store checked before each downstream call
Switch the subscription to at-most-once delivery so duplicate messages become impossible
Retry the downstream call until it succeeds, then ack the message twice
Batch downstream calls so duplicates land in the same HTTP request

questions.q: A broker cluster sits at 80% disk, consumers lag by hours, and producers spike 3x for a day. What likely fails first?
options: Consumer group coordination collapses entirely because member heartbeats begin timing out under load
Producer batching stops working, tripling the request rate to the broker
Retention or disk limits are hit, forcing eviction or producer throttling before lag clears
Partition leaders migrate continuously, halving the cluster's throughput
